rules.quote: Mention disability only when it’s relevant to the content.
rules.violation_condition: A person's disability is mentioned even though it is irrelevant to the content.
when: Applies when deciding whether to mention disability at all.
rules.why: G-1 separates this specific relevance check from the section's broader instruction to focus on the person.

covers.quote: When you are writing about people with disability, focus on the person.
Use respectful and inclusive language that talks to the person – not their difference.
Terms should not identify people without an understanding of personal preference.
Avoid using the disability as an adjective that defines the person, unless that is their preference.
Use person-first language when you don’t understand individual or community preferences.
Describe the person and then the characteristic.
Refer to someone with hearing loss as a ‘person who is deaf or hard of hearing’.
This community calls itself the Deaf community, and encourages others to do the same.
The Deaf community uses the term with a capital letter ‘D’ as a mark of its identity.
Members of the Deaf community might still use deaf with a lowercase ‘d’ to refer to their hearing.
Use people-first language when you refer to a person with mental illness.
Describe the person as ‘having’ mental illness, just as you would for any other illness or injury.
Don’t describe the person as ‘being’ a disease.

parts.quote: person who is deaf or hard of hearing
person who is blind or has low vision
person with mental illness, person with psychosocial disability, person with a psychiatric condition
person with intellectual disability, person with developmental disability
person who uses a wheelchair or mobility device

rules.quote: Use person-first language for Australian Government content, unless user research says otherwise.
rules.violation_condition: Wording defines a person or group by disability or mental illness without an established preference for that wording, or conflicts with an established individual or community language preference.
when: Person-first language is the default when individual or community preferences are not known.
User research establishing a different individual or community preference overrides the default.
A disability adjective can be used when that is the person's preference.
For mental illness, describe the person as having the illness rather than being a disease.
The Deaf community's cultural identity uses ‘Deaf’ with a capital D; lowercase ‘deaf’ can still describe hearing.
rules.why: G-2 and G-4 consolidate the person-first restatements, preference exceptions and mental-illness ‘having’/‘being’ formulations into one check.

covers.quote: You must design accessible content to meet the Digital Service Standard:
Criterion 1. Understand user needs
Criterion 9. Make it accessible

rules.quote: You must make all government content accessible to people with disability.
rules.specification: This passage states an accessibility obligation and names Digital Service Standard criteria, but does not specify the textual tests needed to identify a particular failure. Those requirements must be established before implementing a checker.
rules.violation_condition: Government content lacks an accessible presentation of its information for people with disability.
when: Applies to all government content.
The page also cites the Digital Service Standard's user-needs and accessibility criteria.
rules.why: G-4 consolidates the repeated accessibility obligation; the external criteria are not expanded into invented textual checks.

rules.quote: Use the word ‘disability’ as an uncountable noun.
rules.specification: Apply this to generic descriptions of people, as demonstrated by the rejection of ‘person with a disability’. Do not infer a universal ban on countable uses: the page itself uses ‘learning disabilities’ and ‘a learning disability’ when discussing particular conditions.
rules.violation_condition: A generic reference to a person with disability treats ‘disability’ as countable, such as ‘person with a disability’.
when: Applies to generic references to people with disability.
rules.why: The countability instruction is a distinct check from person-first word order; its scope needs an explicit interpretation rather than an invented universal prohibition.

rules.quote: Don’t say a person is inspirational only because of their disability.
rules.violation_condition: A person is described as inspirational solely because they have disability.
when: The person's disability is the sole basis for describing them as inspirational.
rules.why: G-2 keeps the sole-basis condition with this specific portrayal check rather than creating a general ban on ‘inspirational’.

rules.quote: Don’t write about people as if they are heroes or victims.
rules.specification: Interpret ‘as if’ as stereotyped disability-based framing, not a prohibition on factual accounts of heroic actions or victimisation.
rules.violation_condition: People with disability are stereotypically portrayed as heroes or victims because of disability.
when: Applies to portrayals of people with disability.
rules.why: G-2 keeps the hero and victim framings together as the alternatives expressly prohibited by one instruction.

rules.quote: Avoid euphemisms and made-up terms, such as ‘differently abled’ and ‘handicapable’.
rules.violation_condition: Disability is described using a euphemism or invented label such as ‘differently abled’ or ‘handicapable’.
when: Applies to terms used to describe disability or people with disability.
The named terms are examples, not an exhaustive list.
rules.why: G-2 keeps the named examples within the general euphemism check instead of making a separate rule for each term.

covers.quote: When you are making comparisons, write:

rules.violation_condition: ‘Able-bodied’ is used as the comparison label for a person without disability.
when: Applies when making comparisons involving people with and without disability.
rules.why: G-1 leaves the shared lead-in unmarked as a separate rule; this item supplies a specific preference over a named alternative.

covers.quote: When you are making comparisons, write:

rules.quote: ‘sighted person’ for someone who is not blind
rules.violation_condition: A comparison uses a label other than ‘sighted person’ for someone who is not blind.
when: Applies when labelling someone who is not blind in a comparison involving blindness.
Ordinary grammatical variants, such as ‘sighted people’, retain the prescribed terminology.
rules.why: G-1 leaves the shared lead-in as an introduction; this item supplies the specific comparison label.

covers.quote: When you are making comparisons, write:

rules.quote: ‘hearing person’ for someone who is not deaf.
rules.violation_condition: A comparison uses a label other than ‘hearing person’ for someone who is not deaf.
when: Applies when labelling someone who is not deaf in a comparison involving deafness.
Ordinary grammatical variants, such as ‘hearing people’, retain the prescribed terminology.
rules.why: G-1 leaves the shared lead-in as an introduction; this item supplies the specific comparison label.

covers.quote: Acceptable terms include ‘person who is blind’ and ‘person who has low vision’.

rules.quote: Don’t write ‘the blind’ or ‘person without sight’.
rules.violation_condition: People who are blind are referred to as ‘the blind’ or ‘person without sight’.
when: Applies when these expressions refer to people who are blind.
rules.why: G-2 keeps the two expressly prohibited blindness labels together; G-3 does not turn the acceptable alternatives into additional rules.
